title: Maintainability

stations.name: Naming conventions
facts: A good name is descriptive but still short. Single letters don't say what the data is, and very long names are hard to read.
The computer doesn't care what a variable is called. Good names are for the humans who read and update the code.

questions.q: Which is the best variable name for a running total of scores?
Why do descriptive variable names make code easier to maintain?
questions.a: Anyone reading the code can tell what data each variable holds

stations.name: Commenting
facts: Comments explain the code to people. They are especially useful at the start of each sub-program.
Comments are skipped when the code is translated, so they don't change how the program behaves.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a comment?
questions.a: To explain what a section of code does, for anyone reading it

questions.q: What happens to comments when a program is run?
questions.a: They are ignored by the translator

stations.name: Indentation and white space
facts: Indented lines are inside the structure above them, so you can see the program's structure at a glance. In Python it is required.
Separating sections makes code quicker to scan without spreading it out so much that it's hard to follow.

questions.a: Which lines belong inside a loop, selection statement or sub-program

questions.q: Which is the best use of white space?
questions.a: Blank lines between sub-programs and sections of code

stations.name: Sub-programs
facts: Procedures and functions are written once and called whenever they're needed, and each one can be tested on its own.
With the code in one sub-program, one fix corrects every place it's used. Copies mean five fixes, and it's easy to miss one.

questions.q: What is a benefit of using sub-programs?
questions.a: Code can be reused without being copied, and each part tested separately

questions.q: The same 10 lines appear in five places and contain a bug. How would a sub-program have helped?
questions.a: The bug would only need fixing once, in the sub-program

stations.name: Why maintainability matters
facts: This is the key terminology definition: maintainable code is easy for anyone to understand, fix and change.
In big projects the person fixing the code is rarely the person who wrote it, and they may be working on it years later.

questions.a: Techniques that make code easier to debug, update and maintain

questions.q: Why is maintainability especially important in large projects?
questions.a: Many programmers work on the code, often for years, so others must be able to understand it

stations.name: Refining an algorithm
facts: Each input needs validating before it is used. Changing the output's capitals or removing prompts doesn't make the program more robust.
A type check makes sure the input is a whole number. A range check would then make sure it is between 11 and 19.

questions.q: Which changes would make the locker code program more robust? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Check the house letter is exactly 1 letter from A to D; Check the form group is a number; Check the year group is a whole number from 7 to 11; Check the seat number is a whole number from 1 to 30

questions.q: A student types 'nine' as their year group. Which check would stop this?

final.name: Final challenge: good practice or bad?

questions.q: Sort each habit: is it good practice, or bad practice that makes code hard to maintain?
questions.a: Descriptive variable names like seatNumber = Good practice; Single-letter variable names like t and p = Bad practice; A comment at the start of each sub-program = Good practice; No indentation inside loops = Bad practice; Repeating the same lines instead of using a loop or sub-program = Bad practice; Splitting the program into named sub-programs = Good practice; No blank lines between sub-programs = Bad practice; Accepting input without any validation = Bad practice
